newsitem.title: INDIA: Courtroom drama as India politician awaits arrest.
newsitem.headline: Courtroom drama as India politician awaits arrest.

text.p: A powerful politician who surrendered on Wednesday before a judge in this eastern Indian city waited for his fate to be decided as his lawyers argued for bail in a small, jampacked courtroom.

Laloo Prasad Yadav, the former chief minister of Bihar state, remained standing for 45 minutes as Judge S.K. Lal listened to a lawyer for the federal Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) who wanted the politician detained so he could be interrogated in connection with a $280 million corruption scandal.

The courtroom was packed with politicians, journalists and Yadav's supporters. The courtyard outside was filled to bursting with thousands of people who had managed to evade a paramilitary police cordon shouting slogans in support of Yadav.
"I have come to surrender. I am not in danger," Yadav told his followers before the judge asked him to sit down.
Earlier Yadav drove in a motorcade to the special courtroom set up by the CBI as his supporters shouted "Laloo, we are with you in your struggle".

Yadav's arrest became inevitable after the Supreme Court on Tuesday rejected his appeal against a Bihar court's refusal to grant him "anticipatory bail", allowed under Indian law to people who apprehend arrest.
Yadav was forced to resign last Friday from leadership of Bihar state after weeks of stubborn resistance following his indictment in April by the CBI in the $280 million state farm funds scandal.

The special court had issued non-bailable warrants against Yadav and three other politicians last Friday, but their detention was stayed by the Supreme Court until it had heard the appeal for bail on Tuesday.
Yadav's exit from power has been clouded by his supporters rubber-stamping his wife Rabri Devi, an unschooled housewife, as his successor.
Devi easily won a confidence vote in the state assembly on Monday and has named a mammoth cabinet of 75 ministers.
"Rabri Devi instals mother of all ministries in Bihar," said a front-page report in the Indian Express newspaper on Wednesday.

Parliament's lower house debated the Yadav issue on Tuesday and India's Home (interior) Minister Indrajit Gupta, a communist member of the ruling coalition, admitted to grudging admiration for Yadav's political manoeuvring.

"He is a clever man," Gupta said. "He knows how to tread the constitutional path...(his wife's appointment) took everyone by surprise but there is nothing unconstitutional about it. This country is used to dynastic rule, people have suffered, digested and swallowed it."
The crisis in Bihar has drawn widespread criticism because of the central government's helplessness in forcing an indicted politician from power.
Bihar, home to rich coal and iron-ore mines, is the country's second most populous state and one of its poorest.
Only 38 percent of Bihar's population of 93 million can read or write -- the highest illiteracy rate in India. Less than a quarter of its women are literate.

Electoral violence and political corruption are rampant in the state. Clashes between low-caste peasant rights activists and upper-caste landowners, who maintain powerful private armies, are also common. Bad roads make most of Bihar's villages inaccessible to any central legal authority.
In the early 1980s, several policemen in the state's Bhagalpur town were discovered blinding accused criminals by shoving bicycle spokes and pouring acid into their eyes.
